items.title: 姚班培养-清华大学交叉信息研究院
items.location: 北京市 海淀区 清华大学 信息科学技术楼(FIT楼) 1-208室 100084 电话：010-62781693 传真：
items.summary: 首页 热点新闻 讲座预告 院系概况 院系简介 院长寄语 现任领导 院系沿革 新闻动态 院系动态 媒体聚焦 人员队伍 全职教师 研究系列 荣誉客座 兼职教师 博士后 行政人员 实验员 姚班本科生 姚班培养 姚班招生 研究生 研究生培养 研究生招生 量子中心 中心简介 师资力量 科研概况 量子中心动态 科学研究 组织架构 课题组介绍 研究动态 科研简报 校园生活 学生活动 衣食住行 公开招聘 教师招聘 博士后招聘 职员招聘 校友频道 校友风采 校友俱乐部 校友捐赠 姚班本科生 姚班培养 姚班招生 清华学堂计算机科学实验班 姚班介绍 “清华学堂计算机科学实验班（姚班）”由世界著名计算机科学家姚期智院士于2005年创办，是清华大学培养国际顶尖计算机科学及交叉创新人才的本科生实验班，被誉为“最优秀的本科生和最优秀的本科教育”标杆。 姚班面向科技发展前沿与国家重大需求构建培养体系，以计算机科学、人工智能和量子信息三大前沿专业方向为核心，供学生自主选择发展方向。在培养模式上，姚班独创"因材施教"与"深耕精耕"相结合的教育理念，以理论知识和基础能力为重中之重，实施阶梯式培养计划：前两年着力强化计算机科学基础理论，后两年开展专业领域深度教育。此外，国际化视野是姚班重要办学特色之一，姚期智院士亲自组建了一支由交叉信息院骨干教师构成的国际化师资团队，为学生设计全英文专业课程体系，所有核心课程均以英文授课，从入学起即引导姚班学生适应国际化学术环境，精心打造全方位、多层次的国际学术交流平台，为其走向世界学术舞台打下坚实的基础。 开班近二十年，在姚期智院士的亲力亲为与不懈努力下，姚班为创新人才培养模式的探索树立了突出典范，先后斩获北京市教学成果奖特等、奖国家级教学成果奖一等奖，并得到教育部的充分肯定和大力支持。姚班本科生人才培养成果斐然，截至2026年9月，累计培养近1250名学生，已毕业学生近840名，其中涌现出9位“清华大学本科生特等奖”得主、6位“斯隆研究奖”得主。姚班本科生在读期间科研成果丰厚，截至2026年9月，累计发表论文近680篇，近370人次在计算机科学、人工智能与量子信息领域国际顶级会议上做会议报告，近30人次荣获国际顶会“最佳论文”、“最佳学生论文”、“最佳新人奖”及“焦点论文奖”等荣誉。 绝大多数姚班毕业生选择继续学术深造，逐渐成为信息科学领域的新生代领军力量。姚班校友职

绝大多数姚班毕业生选择继续学术深造，逐渐成为信息科学领域的新生代领军力量。姚班校友职业分布横跨学术界与高新企业两大领域，其中超过半数毕业生扎根国内发展：据不完全统计，已有近65位校友投身高校教职，其中近35位执教于国内一流高校（含学成回国引进人才20余人，其中7人回到清华大学交叉信息研究院任教）。创业领域同样成果瞩目，由姚班毕业生创办的高新企业都已崭露头角，在业界引领此轮全球信息革命创新浪潮。 陈一镭 助理教授 密码学 陈一镭是清华大学交叉信息学院助理教授。在加入清华前他曾任VISA研究院研究员。在2018年他在Ran Canetti教授和Leonid Reyzin教授的指导下获得博士学位。他本科毕业于上海交通大学。陈一镭的主要研究兴趣是密码学，特别是在伪随机，格密码，数论，和量子计算等方向。他的研究成果主要有：1. 建立了多线性映射和代码混淆在格问题上安全实现的基础；2. 提出了证明Fiat-Shamir假设的方法；3. 给出了一个“不可逆群”的构造。更多信息请登陆他的个人主页：http://www.chenyilei.net 杜韬 助理教授 计算机图形学，机器学习，机器人学 清华大学交叉信息研究院助理教授，主要研究方向为计算机图形学，机器学习，机器人学。他的研究工作结合物理仿真、机器学习、数值优化方法理解和设计动力系统，其相关成果广泛发表于图形学和机器学习顶级会议如SIGGRAPH，ICLR，ICML，NeurIPS等。在加入清华之前，他于2021年从MIT计算机系获得博士学位并担任博士后。他于2015和2013年分别从斯坦福大学计算机系和清华大学软件学院获得硕士和学士学位。 房智轩 助理教授 博弈机制设计，区块链系统，平台设计，网络经济学，群体智能 房智轩，清华大学交叉信息研究院助理教授，博士生导师。博士毕业于清华大学交叉信息研究院 （2018），本科毕业于北京大学物理学院 （2013），在加入清华大学之前，曾在香港中文大学任博士后研究员。目前研究专注于博弈机制设计，区块链系统，平台设计，网络经济学，群体智能等。 高阳 助理教授 计算机视觉，强化学习 高阳2014年本科毕业于清华大学计算机系，2019年博士毕业于美国加州大学伯克利分校计算机系，师从Trevor Darrell教授，并与Pieter Abbeel和Sergey Levine等多位教授长期保持合作。高阳的主要研究方向为计算机视觉和强化学习。此前，他2018年于Intel圣何塞总部研究院与Vladlen Koltun博士开展了自动驾驶方面的深度学习研究。2016年，高阳在Google旗下的自动驾驶部门Waymo担任兼职研究员，对Waymo自动驾驶汽车的视觉部分作出重要改进。高阳在CVPR、ICML、NeurIPS、ECCV、ICLR、ICRA等多个高水平学术会议发表多篇论文，谷歌学术引用达1700余次。个人主页：http://people.iiis.tsinghua.edu.cn/~gaoyang/ 贺天行 助理教授 AI安全，AI模拟，AI游戏 贺天行是交叉信息研究院的助理教授。他目前的研究兴趣有AI社会模拟，AI游戏，和AI安全。贺天行的博士学位在MIT获得，师从James Glass。之后他到UW在Yulia Tsvetkov的指导下做了两年博士后。他的硕士在上海交通大学获得，师从俞凯。他的本科在上海交大ACM班就读。在博后期间，他的工作主要在于为了大语言模型相方面的AI安全相关的算法和协议。在博士期间，他的工作在于理解语言模型的工作机理。 侯攀宇 助理教授 离子量子计算；金刚石色心量子信息应用。 侯攀宇，清华大学交叉信息研究院助理教授，博士生导师。他在清华大学取得物理学和博士学位。在博士期间，师从段路明教授研究基于金刚石系统的量子信息和量子调控研究。他的博士后研究是在美国技术标准局（NIST Boulder）从事基于离子阱的量子计算应用。目前，他的研究兴趣和目标是量子信息的物理实现，包括基于离子的大规模量子计算，以及利用金刚石中氮-空穴色心的多体量子模拟和量子传感。他在物理领域的国际期刊上发表了近20篇论文并担任多个期刊的审稿人及客座编辑。 吕凯风 助理教授 机器学习理论，AI安全与对齐，优化 吕凯风将于 2025 年秋季入职清华大学交叉信息研究院任助理教授，目前主要研究方向包括机器学习理论、AI安全与对齐、优化理论与算法。吕凯风于 2019 年毕业于清华大学交叉信息研究院计算机科学实验班（姚班），博士就读于普林斯顿大学，师从 Sanjeev Arora 教授。他在理解深度学习的优化与泛化上做出了基础性贡献，相关研究工作发表于 NeurIPS、ICML、ICLR 等国际顶级会议中。 濮云飞 助理教授 离子阱量子网络、中性原子阵列量子计算 清华大学交叉信息研究院助理教授，博士生导师，主要从事基于冷原子和囚禁离子的量子网络和量子计算实验研究。2012年清华姚班本科毕业，2018年清华交叉信息研究院博士，之后在奥地利因斯布鲁克大学做博士后，访问学者。多次在Nature Photonics, Physical Review Letters, Physical Review X, Science Advances, Nature Communications等国际顶尖物理学期刊上发表文章。 宋一凡 助理教授 密码学 宋一凡是清华大学交叉信息研究院助理教授。2017年毕业于清华大学计算机科学实验班（姚班），2022年获得卡耐基梅隆大学博士学位，导师是Vipul Goyal教授。宋一凡的主要研究兴趣是理论密码学，特别是与多方安全计算相关、隐私电路、无条件安全性相关的研究，目前他已在国际密码学顶会CRYPTO，EUROCRYPT发表文章10余篇。 王禹皓 助理教授 因果推断，实验设计，高维统计，计量经济学 王禹皓，清华大学交叉信息研究院担任助理教授。曾任剑桥大学博士后研究员，毕业于美国麻省理工学院电气工程与计算机科学系博士、硕士，清华大学自动化系学士。王禹皓的主要研究方向包括因果推断、实验设计、高维统计、计量经济学。已有多篇论文发表于Biometrika、Bernoulli、NeruIPS等，截至2022年8月谷歌学术论文引用超过556次。 吴宇恺 助理教授 量子计算的物理实现，量子信息 清华大学交叉信息研究院助理教授，博士生导师。2015年获清华大学物理学士学位，2019年获美国密歇根大学物理博士学位，2019-2021年在清华大学交叉信息研究院从事博士后研究。主要研究方向为量子计算、量子信息的物理实现。 许华哲 助理教授 强化学习， 机器人学， 计算机视觉，计算机触觉 许华哲，清华大学交叉信息院助理教授/博士生导师。美国斯坦福大学博士后，美国加州大学伯克利分校人工智能实验室 (Berkeley AI Research)博士，清华大学电子工程系学士。主要研究方向为机器人学、深度强化学习、计算机视觉、触觉。许华哲博士师从人工智能实验室主任Trevor Darrell教授。博士期间在Facebook AI Research任兼职研究科学家。博士毕业后，许华哲加入了斯坦福大学攻读博士后，主要进行机器人学研究。其发表的RoboCraft, SLBO、End-to-end Driving等工作已经成为领域内开创性工作， 并被MIT Tech Review等媒体报道。许华哲在RSS、NeurIPS、ICML、ICLR、CVPR、ICCV、ECCV、ICRA、IROS等多个高水平学术会议及期刊发表20多篇论文，多次获得口头报告荣誉。 弋力 助理教授 三维计算机视觉，三维深度学习，机器人感知，计算机图形学，几何处理 弋力博士，现任清华大学交叉信息研究院助理教授。他在斯坦福大学取得博士学位，导师为美国两院院士Leonidas J. Guibas教授，毕业后在谷歌研究院任研究科学家。在此之前，他在清华大学电子工程系取得了学士学位。他的研究兴趣涵盖3D感知，计算机图形学和具身人工智能，他的研究目标是使机器人代理具备理解3D世界并与之互动的能力。他在CVPR，ICCV，ECCV，NeurIPS，SIGGRAPH，SIGGRAPH Asia等顶级会议发表二十余篇论文，并担任CVPR 2022领域主席。他的工作在领域内得到广泛关注，引用数达6000+，代表作品包括ShapeNet，光谱图CNN，PointNet++等。 张焕晨 助理教授 数据库管理系统，索引数据结构，数据压缩，云数据库 张焕晨是清华大学交叉信息研究院助理教授。他博士毕业于卡内基梅陇大学计算机系 (师从 Dave Andersen 和 Andy Pavlo)，本科就读于威斯康星大学麦迪逊分校。加入清华前，他在美国Snowflake公司担任博士后研究员。他的科研方向是数据库管理系统。他对索引数据结构，数据压缩，以及云数据库尤其感兴趣。他的论文通常发表在SIGMOD和VLDB等数据库顶会。他是2021年度 SIGMOD Jim Gray Dissertation Award 的获得者，是获得该国际奖项的首位华人。他也是2021年世界人工智能大会云帆奖得主，并以第一作者身份获得2018年度SIGMOD唯一最佳论文。 张景昭 助理教授 优化，机器学习理论， 强化学习， 动力系统， 异常检测 张景昭博士毕业于麻省理工学院计算机科学专业，导师是Suvrit Sra 和 Ali Jadababaie。目前研究主要包含优化算法复杂性分析，机器学习理论与动力系统，以及人工智能应用。张景昭曾获伯克利研究生奖学金，MIT Lim奖学金，MIT人工智能最佳硕士论文，IIIS青年学者奖学金等奖项。 赵行 助理教授 计算机视觉，多模态机器学习，自动驾驶，机器人学习 赵行，清华大学交叉信息院助理教授。美国麻省理工学院计算机与人工智能实验室MIT CSAIL博士，浙江大学竺可桢学院学士。主要研究方向为多模态机器学习，自动驾驶，机器人学。赵行博士师从人工智能与决策AI+D系主任Antonio Torralba教授，专注于视觉和听觉的场景理解。博士期间在Facebook，NVIDIA，MERL任兼职研究员。博士毕业后，赵行于谷歌自动驾驶Waymo Research担任研究科学家，主要研发多传感器学习和运动预测，其发表的VectorNet, TNT, Open Dataset等工作已经成为自动驾驶业界最广泛使用的算法模型和数据集。赵行在CVPR、ICCV、ECCV、NeurIPS、SIGCOMM、ICRA等多个高水平学术会议及期刊发表40多篇论文，谷歌学术引用达8000余次。曾获ICCP最佳论文奖，Snap Research Fellow, 福布斯中国30 Under 30等荣誉。 郑舒冉 助理教授 计算经济学，人工智能，数据估值 郑舒冉是清华大学交叉信息研究院助理教授。她在2022年于哈佛大学取得计算机科学博士学位，后在2023年于卡内基梅隆大学担任博士后研究员。在2022年秋，郑舒冉于谷歌纽约研究院担任博士生研究员。她的主要研究方向为计算经济学，研究目标是利用经济学工具理解数据和信息在计算机科学问题中的价值。她的研究工作发表于EC, NeurIPS, SODA, UAI等国际顶级会议中。 姚奖学金 SINCE 2009 - Yao Award 为了表彰和奖励“姚班”学生在德、智、体、美、劳等全方面的优异表现，特别是在学习和科研上取得的优异成绩和突出成果，我院专门设立了“Yao Award”。 该奖项在每个学年末，对“姚班”三年级的优秀学生颁发，依据参评学生的成绩和其他学术、活动表现，共设立一等奖1-2名，二等奖2-3名，三等奖3-5名，优胜奖若干名。 1~2 一等奖1-2名 2~3 二等奖2-3名 3~5 三等奖3-5名 优秀 毕业生 马雨玮 交叉信息院2022届研究生 导师 | 姚期智 MORE 马雨玮现为中科大上海研究院博士后，他于2016年加入交叉信息院攻读博士学位，导师为孙麓岩副教授，并于2022年1月份获得博士学位，其博士论文被评为“清华大学优秀博士学位论文”。马雨玮的博士论文主要聚焦.... 唐文斌 交叉信息院2010届研究生 导师 | 姚期智 MORE 首届Yao Award获得者，毕业后于2011年和另外两名交叉信息院校友印奇，杨沐共同创立旷视科技。今年是交叉信息院成立十周年，同时亦是旷视科技成立十周年，唐文斌首先祝福交叉信息院十周年快乐并表达了对姚... 马雨玮22 交叉信息院2022届研究生 导师 | 姚期智 MORE 马雨玮现为中科大上海研究院博士后，他于2016年加入交叉信息院攻读博士学位，导师为孙麓岩副教授，并于2022年1月份获得博士学位，其博士论文被评为“清华大学优秀博士学位论文”。马雨玮的博士论文主要聚焦.... 唐文斌22 交叉信息院2010届研究生 导师 | 姚期智 MORE 首届Yao Award获得者，毕业后于2011年和另外两名交叉信息院校友印奇，杨沐共同创立旷视科技。今年是交叉信息院成立十周年，同时亦是旷视科技成立十周年，唐文斌首先祝福交叉信息院十周年快乐并表达了对姚... 姚班动态 10-09 2026 交叉信息院开展2026年暑期思政实践 08-24 2026 热烈欢迎姚班六字班！ 12-15 2025 清华特奖专访 | 李忆唐：智能所及，关怀所至 08-20 2025 热烈欢迎姚班五字班！ 07-09 2025 2025年计算机科学 “成长伙伴”暑期学校成功举办 地址：北京市 海淀区 清华大学 信息科学技术楼(FIT楼) 1-208室 100084 电话：010-62781693 传真： 010-62781693-转2000 邮箱：iiis@mail.tsinghua.edu.cn 版权所有 @ 清华大学交叉信息研究院 TOP

学生活动 衣食住行 公开招聘 教师招聘 博士后招聘 职员招聘 校友频道 校友风采 校友俱乐部 校友捐赠 姚班本科生 姚班培养 姚班招生 清华学堂计算机科学实验班 姚班介绍 “清华学堂计算机科学实验班（姚班）”由世界著名计算机科学家姚期智院士于2005年创办，是清华大学培养国际顶尖计算机科学及交叉创新人才的本科生实验班，被誉为“最优秀的本科生和最优秀的本科教育”标杆。 姚班面向科技发展前沿与国家重大需求构建培养体系，以计算机科学、人工智能和量子信息三大前沿专业方向为核心，供学生自主选择发展方向。在培养模式上，姚班独创"因材施教"与"深耕精耕"相结合的教育理念，以理论知识和基础能力为重中之重，实施阶梯式培养计划：前两年着力强化计算机科学基础理论，后两年开展专业领域深度教育。此外，国际化视野是姚班重要办学特色之一，姚期智院士亲自组建了一支由交叉信息院骨干教师构成的国际化师资团队，为学生设计全英文专业课程体系，所有核心课程均以英文授课，从入学起即引导姚班学生适应国际化学术环境，精心打造全方位、多层次的国际学术交流平台，为其走向世界学术舞台打下坚实的基础。 开班近二十年，在姚期智院士的亲力亲为与不懈努力下，姚班为创新人才培养模式的探索树立了突出典范，先后斩获北京市教学成果奖特等、奖国家级教学成果奖一等奖，并得到教育部的充分肯定和大力支持。姚班本科生人才培养成果斐然，截至2026年9月，累计培养近1250名学生，已毕业学生近840名，其中涌现出9位“清华大学本科生特等奖”得主、6位“斯隆研究奖”得主。姚班本科生在读期间科研成果丰厚，截至2026年9月，累计发表论文近680篇，近370人次在计算机科学、人工智能与量子信息领域国际顶级会议上做会议报告，近30人次荣获国际顶会“最佳论文”、“最佳学生论文”、“最佳新人奖”及“焦点论文奖”等荣誉。 绝大多数姚班毕业生选择继续学术深造，逐渐成为信息科学领域的新生代领军力量。姚班校友职业分布横跨学术界与高新企业两大领域，其中超过半数毕业生扎根国内发展：据不完全统计，已有近65位校友投身高校教职，其中近35位执教于国内一流高校（含学成回国引进人才20余人，其中7人回到清华大学交叉信息研究院任教）。创业领域同样成果瞩目，由姚班毕业生创办的高新企业都已崭露头角，在业界引领此轮全球信息革命创新浪潮。 陈建宇，清华大学交叉信息研究院长聘副教授，博士生导师。他在清华大学取得学士学位，在加州大学伯克利分校取得博士学位，师从美国国家工程院院士、机电控制学科先驱Masayoshi Tomizuka教授。他近年来在机器人学、自动驾驶、强化学习、控制学的交叉领域从事前沿研究。他的研究目标是构建出具备高性能、高智能的高端机器人软硬件系统。他在机器人、人工智能、控制、交通等领域的国际顶级会议和期刊上发表了三十余篇论文，部分论文入围L4DC 2022、IEEE IV 2021、IFAC MECC 2021等国际会议优秀论文奖。他在2021年入选了“福布斯中国30under30”榜单。 陈一镭 助理教授 密码学 陈一镭是清华大学交叉信息学院助理教授。在加入清华前他曾任VISA研究院研究员。在2018年他在Ran Canetti教授和Leonid Reyzin教授的指导下获得博士学位。他本科毕业于上海交通大学。陈一镭的主要研究兴趣是密码学，特别是在伪随机，格密码，数论，和量子计算等方向。他的研究成果主要有：1. 建立了多线性映射和代码混淆在格问题上安全实现的基础；2. 提出了证明Fiat-Shamir假设的方法；3. 给出了一个“不可逆群”的构造。更多信息请登陆他的个人主页：http://www.chenyilei.net 杜韬 助理教授 计算机图形学，机器学习，机器人学 清华大学交叉信息研究院助理教授，主要研究方向为计算机图形学，机器学习，机器人学。他的研究工作结合物理仿真、机器学习、数值优化方法理解和设计动力系统，其相关成果广泛发表于图形学和机器学习顶级会议如SIGGRAPH，ICLR，ICML，NeurIPS等。在加入清华之前，他于2021年从MIT计算机系获得博士学位并担任博士后。他于2015和2013年分别从斯坦福大学计算机系和清华大学软件学院获得硕士和学士学位。 房智轩 助理教授 博弈机制设计，区块链系统，平台设计，网络经济学，群体智能 房智轩，清华大学交叉信息研究院助理教授，博士生导师。博士毕业于清华大学交叉信息研究院 （2018），本科毕业于北京大学物理学院 （2013），在加入清华大学之前，曾在香港中文大学任博士后研究员。目前研究专注于博弈机制设计，区块链系统，平台设计，网络经济学，群体智能等。 高阳 助理教授 计算机视觉，强化学习 高阳2014年本科毕业于清华大学计算机系，2019年博士毕业于美国加州大学伯克利分校计算机系，师从Trevor Darrell教授，并与Pieter Abbeel和Sergey Levine等多位教授长期保持合作。高阳的主要研究方向为计算机视觉和强化学习。此前，他2018年于Intel圣何塞总部研究院与Vladlen Koltun博士开展了自动驾驶方面的深度学习研究。2016年，高阳在Google旗下的自动驾驶部门Waymo担任兼职研究员，对Waymo自动驾驶汽车的视觉部分作出重要改进。高阳在CVPR、ICML、NeurIPS、ECCV、ICLR、ICRA等多个高水平学术会议发表多篇论文，谷歌学术引用达1700余次。个人主页：http://people.iiis.tsinghua.edu.cn/~gaoyang/ 贺天行 助理教授 AI安全，AI模拟，AI游戏 贺天行是交叉信息研究院的助理教授。他目前的研究兴趣有AI社会模拟，AI游戏，和AI安全。贺天行的博士学位在MIT获得，师从James Glass。之后他到UW在Yulia Tsvetkov的指导下做了两年博士后。他的硕士在上海交通大学获得，师从俞凯。他的本科在上海交大ACM班就读。在博后期间，他的工作主要在于为了大语言模型相方面的AI安全相关的算法和协议。在博士期间，他的工作在于理解语言模型的工作机理。 侯攀宇 助理教授 离子量子计算；金刚石色心量子信息应用。 侯攀宇，清华大学交叉信息研究院助理教授，博士生导师。他在清华大学取得物理学和博士学位。在博士期间，师从段路明教授研究基于金刚石系统的量子信息和量子调控研究。他的博士后研究是在美国技术标准局（NIST Boulder）从事基于离子阱的量子计算应用。目前，他的研究兴趣和目标是量子信息的物理实现，包括基于离子的大规模量子计算，以及利用金刚石中氮-空穴色心的多体量子模拟和量子传感。他在物理领域的国际期刊上发表了近20篇论文并担任多个期刊的审稿人及客座编辑。 吕凯风 助理教授 机器学习理论，AI安全与对齐，优化 吕凯风将于 2025 年秋季入职清华大学交叉信息研究院任助理教授，目前主要研究方向包括机器学习理论、AI安全与对齐、优化理论与算法。吕凯风于 2019 年毕业于清华大学交叉信息研究院计算机科学实验班（姚班），博士就读于普林斯顿大学，师从 Sanjeev Arora 教授。他在理解深度学习的优化与泛化上做出了基础性贡献，相关研究工作发表于 NeurIPS、ICML、ICLR 等国际顶级会议中。 濮云飞 助理教授 离子阱量子网络、中性原子阵列量子计算 清华大学交叉信息研究院助理教授，博士生导师，主要从事基于冷原子和囚禁离子的量子网络和量子计算实验研究。2012年清华姚班本科毕业，2018年清华交叉信息研究院博士，之后在奥地利因斯布鲁克大学做博士后，访问学者。多次在Nature Photonics, Physical Review Letters, Physical Review X, Science Advances, Nature Communications等国际顶尖物理学期刊上发表文章。 宋一凡 助理教授 密码学 宋一凡是清华大学交叉信息研究院助理教授。2017年毕业于清华大学计算机科学实验班（姚班），2022年获得卡耐基梅隆大学博士学位，导师是Vipul Goyal教授。宋一凡的主要研究兴趣是理论密码学，特别是与多方安全计算相关、隐私电路、无条件安全性相关的研究，目前他已在国际密码学顶会CRYPTO，EUROCRYPT发表文章10余篇。 王禹皓 助理教授 因果推断，实验设计，高维统计，计量经济学 王禹皓，清华大学交叉信息研究院担任助理教授。曾任剑桥大学博士后研究员，毕业于美国麻省理工学院电气工程与计算机科学系博士、硕士，清华大学自动化系学士。王禹皓的主要研究方向包括因果推断、实验设计、高维统计、计量经济学。已有多篇论文发表于Biometrika、Bernoulli、NeruIPS等，截至2022年8月谷歌学术论文引用超过556次。 吴宇恺 助理教授 量子计算的物理实现，量子信息 清华大学交叉信息研究院助理教授，博士生导师。2015年获清华大学物理学士学位，2019年获美国密歇根大学物理博士学位，2019-2021年在清华大学交叉信息研究院从事博士后研究。主要研究方向为量子计算、量子信息的物理实现。 许华哲 助理教授 强化学习， 机器人学， 计算机视觉，计算机触觉 许华哲，清华大学交叉信息院助理教授/博士生导师。美国斯坦福大学博士后，美国加州大学伯克利分校人工智能实验室 (Berkeley AI Research)博士，清华大学电子工程系学士。主要研究方向为机器人学、深度强化学习、计算机视觉、触觉。许华哲博士师从人工智能实验室主任Trevor Darrell教授。博士期间在Facebook AI Research任兼职研究科学家。博士毕业后，许华哲加入了斯坦福大学攻读博士后，主要进行机器人学研究。其发表的RoboCraft, SLBO、End-to-end Driving等工作已经成为领域内开创性工作， 并被MIT Tech Review等媒体报道。许华哲在RSS、NeurIPS、ICML、ICLR、CVPR、ICCV、ECCV、ICRA、IROS等多个高水平学术会议及期刊发表20多篇论文，多次获得口头报告荣誉。 弋力 助理教授 三维计算机视觉，三维深度学习，机器人感知，计算机图形学，几何处理 弋力博士，现任清华大学交叉信息研究院助理教授。他在斯坦福大学取得博士学位，导师为美国两院院士Leonidas J. Guibas教授，毕业后在谷歌研究院任研究科学家。在此之前，他在清华大学电子工程系取得了学士学位。他的研究兴趣涵盖3D感知，计算机图形学和具身人工智能，他的研究目标是使机器人代理具备理解3D世界并与之互动的能力。他在CVPR，ICCV，ECCV，NeurIPS，SIGGRAPH，SIGGRAPH Asia等顶级会议发表二十余篇论文，并担任CVPR 2022领域主席。他的工作在领域内得到广泛关注，引用数达6000+，代表作品包括ShapeNet，光谱图CNN，PointNet++等。 张焕晨 助理教授 数据库管理系统，索引数据结构，数据压缩，云数据库 张焕晨是清华大学交叉信息研究院助理教授。他博士毕业于卡内基梅陇大学计算机系 (师从 Dave Andersen 和 Andy Pavlo)，本科就读于威斯康星大学麦迪逊分校。加入清华前，他在美国Snowflake公司担任博士后研究员。他的科研方向是数据库管理系统。他对索引数据结构，数据压缩，以及云数据库尤其感兴趣。他的论文通常发表在SIGMOD和VLDB等数据库顶会。他是2021年度 SIGMOD Jim Gray Dissertation Award 的获得者，是获得该国际奖项的首位华人。他也是2021年世界人工智能大会云帆奖得主，并以第一作者身份获得2018年度SIGMOD唯一最佳论文。 张景昭 助理教授 优化，机器学习理论， 强化学习， 动力系统， 异常检测 张景昭博士毕业于麻省理工学院计算机科学专业，导师是Suvrit Sra 和 Ali Jadababaie。目前研究主要包含优化算法复杂性分析，机器学习理论与动力系统，以及人工智能应用。张景昭曾获伯克利研究生奖学金，MIT Lim奖学金，MIT人工智能最佳硕士论文，IIIS青年学者奖学金等奖项。 赵行 助理教授 计算机视觉，多模态机器学习，自动驾驶，机器人学习 赵行，清华大学交叉信息院助理教授。美国麻省理工学院计算机与人工智能实验室MIT CSAIL博士，浙江大学竺可桢学院学士。主要研究方向为多模态机器学习，自动驾驶，机器人学。赵行博士师从人工智能与决策AI+D系主任Antonio Torralba教授，专注于视觉和听觉的场景理解。博士期间在Facebook，NVIDIA，MERL任兼职研究员。博士毕业后，赵行于谷歌自动驾驶Waymo Research担任研究科学家，主要研发多传感器学习和运动预测，其发表的VectorNet, TNT, Open Dataset等工作已经成为自动驾驶业界最广泛使用的算法模型和数据集。赵行在CVPR、ICCV、ECCV、NeurIPS、SIGCOMM、ICRA等多个高水平学术会议及期刊发表40多篇论文，谷歌学术引用达8000余次。曾获ICCP最佳论文奖，Snap Research Fellow, 福布斯中国30 Under 30等荣誉。 郑舒冉 助理教授 计算经济学，人工智能，数据估值 郑舒冉是清华大学交叉信息研究院助理教授。她在2022年于哈佛大学取得计算机科学博士学位，后在2023年于卡内基梅隆大学担任博士后研究员。在2022年秋，郑舒冉于谷歌纽约研究院担任博士生研究员。她的主要研究方向为计算经济学，研究目标是利用经济学工具理解数据和信息在计算机科学问题中的价值。她的研究工作发表于EC, NeurIPS, SODA, UAI等国际顶级会议中。 姚奖学金 SINCE 2009 - Yao Award 为了表彰和奖励“姚班”学生在德、智、体、美、劳等全方面的优异表现，特别是在学习和科研上取得的优异成绩和突出成果，我院专门设立了“Yao Award”。 该奖项在每个学年末，对“姚班”三年级的优秀学生颁发，依据参评学生的成绩和其他学术、活动表现，共设立一等奖1-2名，二等奖2-3名，三等奖3-5名，优胜奖若干名。 1~2 一等奖1-2名 2~3 二等奖2-3名 3~5 三等奖3-5名 优秀 毕业生 马雨玮 交叉信息院2022届研究生 导师 | 姚期智 MORE 马雨玮现为中科大上海研究院博士后，他于2016年加入交叉信息院攻读博士学位，导师为孙麓岩副教授，并于2022年1月份获得博士学位，其博士论文被评为“清华大学优秀博士学位论文”。马雨玮的博士论文主要聚焦.... 唐文斌 交叉信息院2010届研究生 导师 | 姚期智 MORE 首届Yao Award获得者，毕业后于2011年和另外两名交叉信息院校友印奇，杨沐共同创立旷视科技。今年是交叉信息院成立十周年，同时亦是旷视科技成立十周年，唐文斌首先祝福交叉信息院十周年快乐并表达了对姚... 马雨玮22 交叉信息院2022届研究生 导师 | 姚期智 MORE 马雨玮现为中科大上海研究院博士后，他于2016年加入交叉信息院攻读博士学位，导师为孙麓岩副教授，并于2022年1月份获得博士学位，其博士论文被评为“清华大学优秀博士学位论文”。马雨玮的博士论文主要聚焦.... 唐文斌22 交叉信息院2010届研究生 导师 | 姚期智 MORE 首届Yao Award获得者，毕业后于2011年和另外两名交叉信息院校友印奇，杨沐共同创立旷视科技。今年是交叉信息院成立十周年，同时亦是旷视科技成立十周年，唐文斌首先祝福交叉信息院十周年快乐并表达了对姚... 姚班动态 10-09 2026 交叉信息院开展2026年暑期思政实践 08-24 2026 热烈欢迎姚班六字班！ 12-15 2025 清华特奖专访 | 李忆唐：智能所及，关怀所至 08-20 2025 热烈欢迎姚班五字班！ 07-09 2025 2025年计算机科学 “成长伙伴”暑期学校成功举办 地址：北京市 海淀区 清华大学 信息科学技术楼(FIT楼) 1-208室 100084 电话：010-62781693 传真： 010-62781693-转2000 邮箱：iiis@mail.tsinghua.edu.cn 版权所有 @ 清华大学交叉信息研究院 TOP

量子信息是一门新兴的交叉学科领域，涉及计算机科学、信息科学和量子物理，为后摩尔时代提供了新的技术路径，探索了21世纪信息科学发展的新基础与新方法。量子信息技术已成为各国战略竞争的焦点之一。量子信息科学作为量子调控的核心，是信息网络与纳米科学等领域的交叉方向，代表了中国未来科技发展的重要战略方向之一。 清华大学于2011年1月6日正式成立量子信息中心 （Center for Quantum Information, CQI），并于2011年1月15日在清华大学FIT楼报告厅举行了揭牌仪式。该中心由2000年图灵奖得主、世界顶尖计算机科学家姚期智教授领导，旨在建设一个世界级的量子信息教学与科研平台。 姚教授是最早在量子信息领域做出开创性贡献的计算机科学家之一。他的研究兴趣主要集中在计算理论及其在密码学和量子计算中的应用。姚教授因其在计算理论方面的基础性贡献，包括伪随机数生成的复杂性理论、密码学以及通信复杂性等方面的成果，荣获2000年A.M. 图灵奖。他是图灵奖设立以来首位获此殊荣的亚洲学者，其研究成果推动了复杂性理论的发展，并对量子信息科学的进步起到了关键作用。作为网络通信复杂性理论的先驱，姚教授在1993年首次提出了量子通信复杂性模型，为量子计算机的发展奠定了理论基础；1995年，他又提出了分布式量子计算模型，这一模型后来成为分布式量子算法和量子通信协议安全性的基础。 段路明教授现任密歇根大学教授、清华大学姚期智讲座教授，是组建量子信息物理实现团队的主要负责人之一。段教授是该领域的青年领军人物，他在量子网络、量子计算机、远距离量子通信及量子模拟等方面的物理实现研究已对量子信息领域产生了深远而广泛的影响。 量子信息中心借鉴国际一流高校和科研机构的管理机制，目前的研究方向包括全量子网络、量子计算、量子模拟、量子算法与复杂性理论、以及量子操作等。随着中心的进一步发展，其研究与合作也将拓展至更多与量子技术及信息安全相关的领域。 师资力量 姚期智 院长 教授 算法，密码学，量子计算，人工智能 MORE 段路明 清华大学姚期智讲座教授，清华大学基础科学讲席教授 items.title: Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference
items.summary: Back to Articles Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference Enterprise + Article Published November 26, 2026 Upvote 15 +9 Ryan Chesler emelryan Follow nvidia Marek Wawrzos mwawrzos Follow nvidia Steve Han steve-nvidia Follow nvidia We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse , a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents. Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference . We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion. What Parse 3.5 produces Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content.
items.content: Back to Articles Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference Enterprise + Article Published November 26, 2026 Upvote 15 +9 Ryan Chesler emelryan Follow nvidia Marek Wawrzos mwawrzos Follow nvidia Steve Han steve-nvidia Follow nvidia We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse , a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents. Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference . We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion. What Parse 3.5 produces Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications. Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation. This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process. We are open-sourcing three datasets used in the Parse 3.5 training : Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples : rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values. Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples : rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships. OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples : synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading. Each release includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. Use these pairs to fine-tune document models or create new variations for a target document type or language. Figure 2. Parse recovers 18, 27, 39, and 54 from the chart geometry SFT teaches the capability; RLVR improves consistency We trained Parse 3.5 with two phases of training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) spanning text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents. Learning to predict structured targets established the general capability of reading a page and representing its contents. We then continued with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) , using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) . Rewards check the quality of sampled extractions. For example, a chart extraction can earn a better reward for recovering the correct series and values, producing a usable structure, and finishing without repeatedly generating the same content. A difficult page can have several valid representations. These checks give the model flexibility to find a correct answer without prescribing one exact token sequence, while discouraging looping and unfinished output. Figure 3. A controlled comparison of SFT and GRPO with matched evaluation settings. These are development checkpoints, separate from the final released model. Loop counts use a repetition check. Methods . The matched comparison shows the benefit: loop-flagged outputs fall from 126 to 29 pages—about 77% fewer —and outputs reaching the 9,000-token limit fall from 185 to 35 . Overall score improves from 66.24 to 71.38 , including +5.18 points in tables and +4.15 in charts . Faster inference through architecture and DFlash2 A parser must generate substantial text and structure for every page. Alongside the training work, we optimized how Parse 3.5 processes images and decodes those outputs. Component Parse 2.0 Parse 3.5 Page preprocessing Fixed 2048 × 1664 canvas NaViT dynamic rectangular inputs Image-to-text connection Encoder–decoder cross-attention Compressed visual tokens as a causal prefix Decoder self-attention Multi-head attention GQA-8: 16 query heads, 8 key/value heads Speculative decoding One-token lookahead (MTP); optional DFlash2 NaViT preprocessing adapts the input shape to the page. A visual adapter compresses the image sequence, and the text decoder consumes it as a prefix, replacing encoder–decoder cross-attention. Grouped-query attention with eight key/value heads (GQA-8) reduces the decoder’s attention-cache memory. The built-in multi-token prediction (MTP) head supplies one-token lookahead. Our DFlash2 speculator goes further: a small draft model proposes up to 32 tokens ahead , and Parse verifies the proposals together. In the measured 32-token configuration, it averages about 14 accepted draft tokens , or roughly 15 output tokens of progress per verification step including the target token. Figure 4. Native single-pass throughput on one H200, BF16, using the same 2,078 pages. Parse 2.0 uses one trial per point; Parse 3.5 shows three-trial medians. Arrows show the gain from Parse 3.5 base to DFlash2. Measurement details . In the native single-pass benchmark on one H200 in BF16, DFlash2 increased throughput 7.62× at concurrency 1 and 1.52× at concurrency 512, compared with Parse 3.5 with speculative decoding disabled. At 512, Parse 3.5 reaches 13.48 pages/s without speculation and 20.44 pages/s with DFlash2, versus 2.98 for Parse 2.0. Those are 4.53× and 6.86× the Parse 2.0 throughput, respectively. Fast parsing gives us room to revisit difficult regions. Start with a full-page prediction, then add focused reprocessing where the document needs it: Single pass - Parse the full page once for text, layout, tables, and charts. Double pass - use for dense tables and small chart details. Crop the table and chart regions found by the parser, re-parse them at higher detail, and merge the refinements into the page output. Triple pass - Instead of only using the models full page parsing bounding boxes, use a second pass of the model in detection mode in order to get verification that all boxes have been accurately found and text has not been missed and re-extract any found charts or tables in a third pass Figure 5. Additional stages focus computation on difficult regions. Multiple crops can require multiple requests. In the published reference evaluation, double and triple pass add 2.18 and 2.46 ParseBench points over single pass. The additional work lets applications trade some throughput for better extraction in difficult regions. Reference results and serving measurements . Apply the same SFT/RLVR approach to your documents We are sharing a Parse fine-tuning recipe that takes developers through paired data generation, NeMo Automodel SFT , and NeMo RL GRPO , using vLLM to generate candidate answers. The worked example uses a synthetic dental form with an odontogram : a chart showing teeth, planned procedures, and affected tooth surfaces. Before adaptation, Parse reads the printed tooth numbers but misses the intended procedure table. SFT teaches it to associate each marked tooth with a procedure and its placement on the tooth. Figure 6. A recorded recipe example: after SFT, all six chart rows match the target. Full image and native training label . RLVR then reinforces accuracy and consistent completion. In the dental reference run, the estimated first-attempt success rate (sampled pass@1) rose from 0.00% for the base model to 95.85% after SFT and 96.58% after RLVR. Figure 7. Matched evaluation on 256 held-out forms from the same synthetic generator, with eight samples per page. Success requires natural completion, exact chart content, and error-free normalized page text. Evaluation protocol . To adapt the recipe, supply your own image/label pairs and a verifier: checks that determine whether an extraction is correct. The included document reward components cover text fidelity, bounding boxes, tables, chart facts, and completion. Combine the components relevant to your task, add schema checks, and use completion and repetition checks to discourage looping or unfinished output. We are excited that the community has extended and improved Parse for Thai , Persian/Farsi , and Arabic already and we hope that these additional datasets and fine-tuning recipes will help encourage these efforts and future models. We thank Denis Ovchinnikov for his work on vLLM integration and independent performance validation, Oliver Holworthy for improving the fine-tuning recipe's runtime setup and reproducibility, and Bo Liu for technical review. items.raw_text: Back to Articles Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference Enterprise + Article Published November 26, 2026 Upvote 15 +9 Ryan Chesler emelryan Follow nvidia Marek Wawrzos mwawrzos Follow nvidia Steve Han steve-nvidia Follow nvidia We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse , a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents. Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference . We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion. What Parse 3.5 produces Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications. Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation. This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process. We are open-sourcing three datasets used in the Parse 3.5 training : Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples : rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values. Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples : rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships. OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples : synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading. Each release includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. Use these pairs to fine-tune document models or create new variations for a target document type or language. Figure 2. Parse recovers 18, 27, 39, and 54 from the chart geometry SFT teaches the capability; RLVR improves consistency We trained Parse 3.5 with two phases of training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) spanning text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents. Learning to predict structured targets established the general capability of reading a page and representing its contents. We then continued with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) , using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) . Rewards check the quality of sampled extractions. For example, a chart extraction can earn a better reward for recovering the correct series and values, producing a usable structure, and finishing without repeatedly generating the same content. A difficult page can have several valid representations. These checks give the model flexibility to find a correct answer without prescribing one exact token sequence, while discouraging looping and unfinished output. Figure 3. A controlled comparison of SFT and GRPO with matched evaluation settings. These are development checkpoints, separate from the final released model. Loop counts use a repetition check. Methods . The matched comparison shows the benefit: loop-flagged outputs fall from 126 to 29 pages—about 77% fewer —and outputs reaching the 9,000-token limit fall from 185 to 35 . Overall score improves from 66.24 to 71.38 , including +5.18 points in tables and +4.15 in charts . Faster inference through architecture and DFlash2 A parser must generate substantial text and structure for every page. Alongside the training work, we optimized how Parse 3.5 processes images and decodes those outputs. Component Parse 2.0 Parse 3.5 Page preprocessing Fixed 2048 × 1664 canvas NaViT dynamic rectangular inputs Image-to-text connection Encoder–decoder cross-attention Compressed visual tokens as a causal prefix Decoder self-attention Multi-head attention GQA-8: 16 query heads, 8 key/value heads Speculative decoding One-token lookahead (MTP); optional DFlash2 NaViT preprocessing adapts the input shape to the page. A visual adapter compresses the image sequence, and the text decoder consumes it as a prefix, replacing encoder–decoder cross-attention. Grouped-query attention with eight key/value heads (GQA-8) reduces the decoder’s attention-cache memory. The built-in multi-token prediction (MTP) head supplies one-token lookahead. Our DFlash2 speculator goes further: a small draft model proposes up to 32 tokens ahead , and Parse verifies the proposals together. In the measured 32-token configuration, it averages about 14 accepted draft tokens , or roughly 15 output tokens of progress per verification step including the target token. Figure 4. Native single-pass throughput on one H200, BF16, using the same 2,078 pages. Parse 2.0 uses one trial per point; Parse 3.5 shows three-trial medians. Arrows show the gain from Parse 3.5 base to DFlash2. Measurement details . In the native single-pass benchmark on one H200 in BF16, DFlash2 increased throughput 7.62× at concurrency 1 and 1.52× at concurrency 512, compared with Parse 3.5 with speculative decoding disabled. At 512, Parse 3.5 reaches 13.48 pages/s without speculation and 20.44 pages/s with DFlash2, versus 2.98 for Parse 2.0. Those are 4.53× and 6.86× the Parse 2.0 throughput, respectively. Fast parsing gives us room to revisit difficult regions. Start with a full-page prediction, then add focused reprocessing where the document needs it: Single pass - Parse the full page once for text, layout, tables, and charts. Double pass - use for dense tables and small chart details. Crop the table and chart regions found by the parser, re-parse them at higher detail, and merge the refinements into the page output. Triple pass - Instead of only using the models full page parsing bounding boxes, use a second pass of the model in detection mode in order to get verification that all boxes have been accurately found and text has not been missed and re-extract any found charts or tables in a third pass Figure 5. Additional stages focus computation on difficult regions. Multiple crops can require multiple requests. In the published reference evaluation, double and triple pass add 2.18 and 2.46 ParseBench points over single pass. The additional work lets applications trade some throughput for better extraction in difficult regions. Reference results and serving measurements . Apply the same SFT/RLVR approach to your documents We are sharing a Parse fine-tuning recipe that takes developers through paired data generation, NeMo Automodel SFT , and NeMo RL GRPO , using vLLM to generate candidate answers. The worked example uses a synthetic dental form with an odontogram : a chart showing teeth, planned procedures, and affected tooth surfaces. Before adaptation, Parse reads the printed tooth numbers but misses the intended procedure table. SFT teaches it to associate each marked tooth with a procedure and its placement on the tooth. Figure 6. A recorded recipe example: after SFT, all six chart rows match the target. Full image and native training label . RLVR then reinforces accuracy and consistent completion. In the dental reference run, the estimated first-attempt success rate (sampled pass@1) rose from 0.00% for the base model to 95.85% after SFT and 96.58% after RLVR. Figure 7. Matched evaluation on 256 held-out forms from the same synthetic generator, with eight samples per page. Success requires natural completion, exact chart content, and error-free normalized page text. Evaluation protocol . To adapt the recipe, supply your own image/label pairs and a verifier: checks that determine whether an extraction is correct. The included document reward components cover text fidelity, bounding boxes, tables, chart facts, and completion. Combine the components relevant to your task, add schema checks, and use completion and repetition checks to discourage looping or unfinished output. We are excited that the community has extended and improved Parse for Thai , Persian/Farsi , and Arabic already and we hope that these additional datasets and fine-tuning recipes will help encourage these efforts and future models. We thank Denis Ovchinnikov for his work on vLLM integration and independent performance validation, Oliver Holworthy for improving the fine-tuning recipe's runtime setup and reproducibility, and Bo Liu for technical review. items.content: Algorithms and theory Google’s mission presents many exciting algorithmic and optimization challenges across different product areas including Search, Ads, Social, and Google Infrastructure. These include optimizing internal systems such as scheduling the machines that power the numerous computations done each day, as well as optimizations that affect core products and users, from online allocation of ads to page-views to automatic management of ad campaigns, and from clustering large-scale graphs to finding best paths in transportation networks. Other than employing new algorithmic ideas to impact millions of users, Google researchers contribute to the state-of-the-art research in these areas by publishing in top conferences and journals. Recent Publications See More The Visibility VC-Dimension of Simple Polygons is Six Dror Aiger Sariel Har-Peled 2027 Preview Preview abstract We prove that no simple polygon P ⊂ R 2 contains a visibility-shattered set of seven points, establishing that the maximum visibility VC-dimension over all simple polygons is six. Combined with Valtr’s lower bound [Val98], this resolves the visibility VC-dimension problem for simple polygons, improving the upper bound of 23 due to Valtr [Val98] and 14 due to Gilbers and Klein [GK14] to the exact value 6. We also exhibit an explicit 968-vertex simple polygon with rational vertex coordinates that shatters six points in strictly convex position, confirming maxP VC-dim(P) = maxP VC-dimconvex(P) = 6. Our proof combines a general-position perturbation, a structural decomposition of the convex hull of a shattered seven-point set into a contiguous block of certified front vertices and non-certified hull vertices, an extended polygonenclosure calculus, and a sound chirotope reduction whose geometric soundness implications are machine-checked in Lean 4 and independently verified via Z3 real-arithmetic proofs and dual CDCL SAT solvers. View details Hadwiger’s Covering Conjecture in Three Dimensions Dror Aiger Sariel Har-Peled Goran Žužić 2027 Preview Preview abstract Let K in R^3 be an arbitrary convex body, that is, a compact convex subset of R^3 with nonempty interior. We prove unconditionally that K can be covered by eight smaller positive homothetic copies of itself: there exist a scalar lambda in (0, 1) and translation vectors v_1, ..., v_8 in R^3 such that K is contained in the union of (lambda K + v_i) for i = 1, ..., 8. This resolves Hadwiger's covering conjecture in three dimensions. The proof works in Boltyanski's equivalent boundary illumination formulation and is completely self-contained. Parallelepipeds are covered directly by eight translates of (2/3)K. For any convex body K that is not a parallelepiped, we place its centrally symmetric halved difference body S = (1/2)(K - K) in John's position (B^3 subseteq S) and show that the spherical average of its support function satisfies 8 int_{S^2} h_S d sigma_tilde < 12, with equality only for orthogonal cubes. Using outer polyhedral approximations together with Cauchy's planar perimeter formula, the full spherical measure of directions not parallel to any boundary segment of K, and lower semicontinuity of curve variation, we find a unit vector w_* in S^2 whose shadow boundary Sigma(K, w_*) on K itself is a continuous closed curve of S-length strictly less than 12. Splitting Sigma(K, w_*) into six contiguous arcs of S-length strictly less than 2 and applying Helly's theorem in R^3 illuminates each arc with one direction, while +-w_* illuminate the remainder of partial K. The proof was discovered using an experimental harness on top of Gemini 4 Carbon and formally verified in Lean 4. View details Depth-CoT Tradeoffs in Transformers: A Look at Path Following Clayton Sanford Matus Telgarsky Justin D. Li 2027 Preview Preview abstract Modern transformers have been scaled up in size, data, training-time compute, and more recently test-time compute based on Chain-of-Thought (CoT), but the consequences of trading off these parameters are unknown. We construct explicit tradeoffs between two of these aspects: the number of layers in a transformer and the number of CoT tokens. Our first result is general: with mild assumptions and a single-token prompt, for any integer k, a transformer using soft attention and SwiGLU MLP layers with L layers and n CoT tokens can be converted to a transformer with at most ckL layers and ⌈n/k⌉ CoT tokens, and vice versa, although with an increase to the size of other parameters. We then a multi-token prompt path following task, finding that additional preprocessing from the multi-token prompt changes the depth-CoT relationship in this case. We construct an attention-only network with L layers and 2^(L−2) heads that can traverse 2^(L−1) − 1 edges along a path with a single CoT token, demonstrating at least an exponential relationship between increases in depth and reductions in the number of CoT tokens needed to traverse the entire path. This relationship for the path following task holds empirically as well, as demonstrated by training networks with up to 5 layers, with the tradeoff between depth and the maximum number of edge traversals in a single CoT token exactly matching our theoretical constructions. View details Geo-Contextual AI Concierge: Minimizing Internal Support Friction Through Proactive Knowledge Synthesis Neeraj Choudhary Dónal Doyle Technical Report (2026) Preview Preview abstract In large-scale distributed enterprises, traditional Knowledge Management (KM) systems face a critical failure mode: static documentation cannot keep pace with evolving operational realities and regional nuances. This "knowledge latency" forces employees out of self-service workflows and into costly support ticketing queues. This paper introduces SENTINEL, a geo-contextual AI framework designed to shift enterprise support from reactive retrieval to proactive interception. The architecture employs a novel dual-engine system integrated into an omni-present interface. The first engine utilizes Large Language Models (LLMs) to conduct pre-emptive, historical case-grounded audits of documentation, generating a "Contextual Density" score that identifies friction zones. The second engine is an autonomous Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) agent that surfaces in-situ via a location-intelligent assistant window, resolving queries in real-time. By functioning as a strategic "defensive barrier" at the point of origin, SENTINEL demonstrates how a proactive AI assistant can drive high-fidelity, in-situ case deflection. View details Cardio Load in exercise and everyday life: A modified TRIMP metric for continuously-sensing consumer wearables Justin Phillips Daniel Roggen YongSuk Cho Robert Harle Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise (2026) Preview Preview abstract PURPOSE: To introduce Cardio Load (CL), a metric quantifying cardiovascular work from all activities across the day, and to investigate its distribution by age, gender, and workout profiles. CL adapts the Training Impulse (TRIMP) model by leveraging continuous heart rate and movement data from wearables, enabling minute-level intensity estimation. We also discuss the derivation of weekly target loads, intended to guide fitness maintenance. METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 31.2 million hours of wrist-worn wearable data collected over a six-week period. The dataset comprised a 40,000-subject subset (37.9% female) of consenting Google Pixel Watch® users in the United States, aged 18 to 80 years (18-39: 41.8%, 40-59: 43.5%, 60+: 14.6%). Measured data included minute-interval heart rate averages, resting and maximum heart rates, minute-interval averaged accelerometer log energy, and manually-logged or auto-detected activity types. Cardio Load scores and target loads were calculated daily for each subject and compared across age and gender. We also compared the proportions of CL gained during workouts and incidental daily activities for these groups. RESULTS: Overall, the study population's mean ± SD weekly CL scores were 221 ± 156 (female) and 259 ± 169 (male). Median weekly Cardio Load (CL) values exhibited consistency for individuals between 30 and 75 years of age. When analyzed in five-year age groups, the coefficient of variation (CV%) of median weekly CL values within this age range was less than 4.5%, with younger and older subjects demonstrating higher and lower median CL, respectively. The median proportion of CL accumulated during structured workouts versus incidental daily activity was 41.0% (female) and 49.0% (male) for all subjects, though this varied considerably with average weekly workout duration. CV% of weekly target load and daily target load over 6 weeks was 23.6% and 35.2% respectively. CONCLUSION: Cardio Load provides a continuous quantification of activity load from wearables, acknowledging both structured workouts and everydayincidental activity. CL is equitably rewarded for age ranges spanning 30-75 years. Weekly target loads were found to have little measurement variability and be more consistent and, consequently, more practical for planning training and physical activity than daily targets. View details Distributional Alignment Games for Answer-Level Fine-Tuning Mehryar Mohri Jon Schneider Yifan Wu ICML 2026 Preview Preview abstract We focus on the problem of \emph{Answer-Level Fine-Tuning} (ALFT), where the goal is to optimize a language model based on the correctness or properties of its final answers, rather than the specific reasoning traces used to produce them. Directly optimizing answer-level objectives is computationally intractable due to the need to marginalize over the vast space of latent reasoning paths. To overcome this, we propose a general game-theoretical framework that lifts the problem to a \emph{Distributional Alignment Game}. We formulate ALFT as a two-player game between a Policy (the generator) and a Target (an auxiliary distribution). We prove that the Nash Equilibrium of this game corresponds exactly to the solution of the original answer-level optimization problem. items.title: The AI Act Advisory Forum holds its second meeting

items.content: The second meeting of the AI Act Advisory Forum took place, in hybrid format, on Monday 16 November in Brussels. ©AdobeStock Nataliya One of the highlights of the meeting was the election of the two co-Chairs. Mrs Laura Lázaro Cabrera and Mrs Catarina Nunes Santos were elected. Both co-Chairs have taken on the responsibility of leading the Forum and representing its views for the next two years. Mrs Laura Lázaro Cabrera, representing the non-commercial views of the Forum, is Director of the Equity and Data programme and Deputy Director and Counsel to the Center for Democracy and Technology (CDT) Europe in Brussels, where she leads the work promoting the effective protection of fundamental human rights in the implementation of European Union legislation regulating new technologies. Mrs Catarina Santos Nunes, representing the commercial views of the Forum, is the Chief Operating Officer and Chief Compliance Office at Starkdata. Starkdata is a Portuguese company and provides an AI-powered predictive analytics platform which enables businesses to make data-driven decisions. Forum members adopted the Forum's Rule of Procedure, giving the Forum a clear framework for its functioning and for its decision-making process. Items discussed The meeting was kicked off with presentations from the AI Office. Updates on the current work of the AI Office were shared, and included insights on its enforcement activities, its work on innovation, the EU KIDS Act, and the Action Plan on Cybersecurity and AI. Discussions on the stocktaking on technological developments of AI, covering the latest developments in terms of AI capabilities, incidents as well as industrial application and AI R&D automation, also took place. The Chair of the AI Board , Mrs Jean Carberry, the Chair and the Vice-Chair of the Scientific Panel , Mr Seán Ó hÉigeartaigh, and Nicolas Moës, gave Advisory Forum participants information on their two respective bodies, exploring the synergies between the Advisory Forum, the AI Board and the Scientific Panel, the governance bodies established under the EU AI Act. The Advisory Forum was presented with possible work streams on which the AI Office wishes to seek its advice. Members were invited to discuss one of two topics: AI companions or AI agents, as well as the future of its work. The discussions took place in breakout groups, which subsequently reported to the plenary, sharing their main conclusions on both topics. More on the AI Act Advisory Forum Related content News article 19 June 2026 The AI Act Advisory Forum convenes its kick-off meeting On 19 June, the Commission hosted the inaugural session of the AI Act Advisory Forum, the general advisory body to the European Commission and the AI Board, supporting the implementation and enforcement of the AI Act. Last update 24 November 2026 Print as PDF

items.content: Back to Articles Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost Published November 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 158 +152 Younes B ybelkada Follow ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow Nathan Habib SaylorTwift Follow Lysandre lysandre Follow Amine Dirhoussi aminediroHF Follow Adithya S K AdithyaSK Follow shaun smith evalstate Follow Sergio Paniego sergiopaniego Follow Joel Niklaus joelniklaus Follow Lewis Tunstall lewtun Follow Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution. Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination. Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time. Our earlier work ( multi-harness RL , harness adapters ) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations. TL;DR We trained one LoRA adapter for Qwen3.8-27B per agent harness (pi, Hermes Agent, OpenCode), with RL inside the harness itself. Datasets, training and agent rollouts all happen on the Hub in Jobs using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer , OpenEnv and harbor. Each harness adapter beats the base model under its own harness on both benchmarks, for both performance and efficiency. The three LoRAs are also merged into a single super adapter that runs unchanged under pi, Hermes Agent and OpenCode. All artifacts (adapters, GGUFs, RL tasks, safeagents plugin) can be browsed through this Hugging Face collection . Table of Contents Training inside agent harnesses Generating custom RL tasks on Hugging Face Testing the filters with short training runs AsyncGRPOTrainer for more efficient GRPO training Training setup Super-adapter: merging all adapters into one Final results Open question: What did the model really learn to do? Closing words and future directions Training inside agent harnesses We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2 , OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6 . The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol: Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop , SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM 's agent and environment classes, slime 's custom rollout functions, or ART 's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer. Generating custom RL tasks on Hugging Face For this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv . We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains. RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything. This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate , and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B. Three sources Each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves: SWE-smith ( Python , Go ) injects bugs into real Python and Go repositories, with an LLM rewrite or a mutation such as a flipped operator. The tests that catch each bug become the task's tests. It adds volume. SWE-Gym, packaged as Harbor tasks in TaskTrove , turns real GitHub issues and their merged fixes into tasks. It adds real-world bugs. Tasksmith generates tasks from merged pull requests. An LLM agent writes the instruction and tests, and Tasksmith checks the result: the reference and a valid alternative must pass, while the unfixed code and a known-wrong solution must fail. We used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest. Validation with openenv validate A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials: The reference solution earns the maximum reward ( semantic.oracle_max ). Doing nothing scores clearly lower ( semantic.floor_gap ). No canary scores more than doing nothing ( semantic.canary_floor ). A replay of the reference gives the same reward ( runtime.episode_determinism ). Each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task: openenv validate path/to/task --sandbox hf-sandbox 858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded. Difficulty check with the base model A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository. Of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks. Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all. This example shows how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation. Testing the filters with short training runs The pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1. Each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer , on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered: Unvalidated : 24 accepted tasks plus 8 that failed validation. Validated : 32 accepted tasks, chosen without regard to difficulty. Unqualified : 32 accepted tasks that the base model always or never solves. Qualified : 32 accepted tasks that the base model solves on some attempts. The figure below shows how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status. The dataset harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below shows what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config. Source Task type Tasks Qualified SWE-smith Injected bugs in Python and Go 717 144 SWE-Gym (TaskTrove) Real GitHub issues 130 27 Tasksmith Generated from merged pull requests 24 22 Total 871 171 AsyncGRPOTrainer for more efficient GRPO training We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step. For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost . Training setup To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer . The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison. The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which showed that 0.1 worked best). We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then showed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs. Training infrastructure Each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below shows the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes). As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step. Final mixture The final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade . In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below: Before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture. safeagents in the loop We also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup. The number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter. Super-adapter: merging all adapters into one Merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness? We started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere. We concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat" ). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging ( task arithmetic , TIES , KnOTS ) finds that scaling each update below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters: ⅓ (the average): each harness keeps only a third of its own update. ½: each update at half strength. 1 (the plain sum): every update applied in full. Weight pi hermes opencode All three harnesses Tool calls per task base model 39.1% 46.0% 44.8% 43.3% 49.2 ⅓ (average) 49.4% 51.2% 47.1% 49.2% 35.6 ½ 48.8% 53.5% 55.2% 52.5% 25.9 1 (sum) 40.2% 62.8% 47.1% 50.0% 13.4 The plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own update. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½. Adapter merging evaluation results Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model): Harness Benchmark Qwen3.8-27B Qwen3.8-27B-<harness>-adapted Qwen3.8-27B-super-adapter Qwen3.8-27B , thinking Qwen3.8-27B-super-adapter , thinking pi SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 40.0% 64.0% (−60%) 46.0% (−73%) 74.0% 74.0% (−48%) hermes SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 29.4% 43.1% (−56%) 47.1% (−60%) 45.1% 60.8% (−36%) opencode SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 35.3% 51.0% (−72%) 45.1% (−63%) 47.1% 66.7% (−31%) pi Terminal-Bench 2.1 40.0% 56.5% (−56%) 48.2% (−56%) 52.9% 57.6% (−25%) hermes Terminal-Bench 2.1 44.7% 58.8% (−70%) 55.3% (−53%) 58.8% 63.5% (−19%) opencode Terminal-Bench 2.1 47.6% 52.4% (−53%) 52.4% (−68%) 54.9% 58.5% (−22%) "Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off. With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001). Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties. Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist. The super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same. The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card . Final results This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses. Training results Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens. During training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets new tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below. On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked. Evaluation results This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check. Evaluation setup We evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi automatically applies context compaction, while OpenCode and Hermes don't, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions. Every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval. For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks. For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories . Final evaluation results All three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035). The adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section ). Each model card has the full paired results. Does the efficiency and performance ability transfer across harnesses? To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode. Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses. Evaluation on out-of-distribution tasks and setup What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with? We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with? Results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it. Model pass@1 (all assertions met) vs base Partial credit (share of assertions met) vs base base 23.0% 62.2% pi 160 27.0% +4.0 66.2% +4.0 opencode 150
